# Mugging
Mugging is a colloquial term for a specific type of robbery – it refers to an assault or threat of violence against a person in public, committed with the intent to steal their money or valuables. In a mugging, the perpetrator confronts the victim face-to-face (as opposed to crimes like burglary which involve no direct confrontation) and uses or threatens force to obtain possessions. Legally, most jurisdictions do not define “mugging” as a separate offense; it is usually prosecuted under statutes for robbery (the felonious taking of property from someone through force or intimidation). Mugging is therefore a form of robbery – often called street robbery or strong-arm robbery – distinguished by occurring in a public or semi-public place and involving a sudden personal attack on the victim.
## Terminology and Legal Status
The term “mugging” is informal and does not appear as an official legal category in many countries. For example, in the United Kingdom the word mugging was popularized by the media in the early 1970s; there was no crime formally called “mugging” in British law or crime statistics prior to that period. Law enforcement instead classifies such incidents as robbery or aggravated theft from the person. Similarly, in the United States, a mugging is generally charged as robbery (or as armed robbery if a weapon is used, or aggravated robbery if serious injury or a deadly weapon is involved). These are felony offenses that carry severe penalties, including long prison terms. For instance, a mugger who uses a firearm may face an armed robbery charge with significantly harsher sentencing than simple theft. In contrast to burglary – which involves unlawful entry into a building to commit a crime and does not require a face-to-face confrontation – mugging entails direct interaction with and intimidation of the victim in an open environment.
## Etymology and History
The word mugging in the context of crime originates from 19th-century slang. The verb to mug was used by 1818 to mean “to strike someone’s face,” deriving from mug as a slang term for “face”. By the mid-19th century, mugging was recorded as meaning a beating or physical assault (attested in 1846), and later it came to specifically denote a violent robbery from a person – one early citation from 1939 uses mugging to mean a street robbery with force. The usage likely evolved from the idea of attacking someone’s face or “mug,” as well as from thieves’ slang where mug could mean a gullible victim.
Street robbery itself long predates the modern term. In Victorian Britain, a type of robbery known as garrotting – in which an assailant would choke the victim from behind while an accomplice rifled the victim’s pockets – became notorious in the 1860s. This crime was roughly synonymous with what would today be called mugging. A spate of garrotting incidents in London in 1862 sparked public alarm and a “garrotting panic,” leading to public measures such as anti-garrotte collars and increased street policing.
The term mugging itself gained common usage in American English by the early 20th century and was later adopted into British English. In the early 1970s, British news media began heavily reporting on “muggings” – a new term at the time in the UK – to describe a perceived surge of violent street robberies. Between 1972 and 1973, newspapers warned of a wave of “robberies following sudden attacks in the open,” which they labeled as mugging. This intense coverage created a widespread public impression of a crime wave. Criminologists, such as sociologist Stuart Hall, later argued that the UK had experienced a moral panic over mugging: the media and political rhetoric had amplified fears disproportionately, given that the statistical increase in street robberies was not as drastic as portrayed. The moral panic around mugging in the 1970s also had racial and social dimensions in Britain, as the crime was frequently associated in press reports with young black male perpetrators, raising debates about crime, policing, and prejudice at the time. Despite these controversies, mugging entered the general vocabulary in the UK and elsewhere as a term for street robbery.
## Methods and Characteristics
Muggings are typically opportunistic crimes that occur in public or semi-public spaces such as streets, sidewalks, alleyways, parking lots, parks, or public transit areas. The perpetrator (or group of perpetrators) usually targets a lone individual, often choosing victims who appear to be vulnerable, distracted, or otherwise easy to overpower. Common tactics include element of surprise and intimidation. For example, a mugger may approach the victim suddenly from behind or the side, threaten them with a weapon or physical harm, and demand wallets, purses, phones, jewelry, or other valuable personal items. If the victim does not immediately comply, the mugger might use violence to subdue them. Because muggings involve direct confrontation, victims often face a loss of control and a sudden threat to personal safety, which is why this crime tends to instill high levels of fear in the public.
Modus operandi: Criminologists classify the methods of street robbery into a few broad types:
Confrontation: The mugger directly confronts the victim with a demand or threat at the outset (for example, verbal commands like “Give me your money!” while displaying a threatening posture or weapon). If the victim hesitates or resists, the robber may escalate to force. This is one of the most common approaches.
Blitz attack: The offender uses force immediately – a sudden, violent ambush to disable or disorient the victim before any demand is made. For instance, the mugger may strike or tackle the person without warning and proceed to grab their property. This method aims to overwhelm the victim and prevent resistance.
Con (distraction): The robber tricks the victim to lower their guard. A classic example is asking for the time, directions, or engaging in small talk, thereby distracting the victim, then launching the attack when the victim is off-guard. By using a ruse, the offender can get close to the victim without arousing alarm.
Snatch-theft: Rather than a prolonged confrontation, the thief swiftly grabs an item and flees. This can be considered a subset of mugging when force or the threat of force is involved. A typical scenario is a robber running past someone and yanking away a purse or phone (sometimes called a purse-snatching). If no force is used beyond the snatching action, police might categorize it as a theft from person; however, if the victim is jostled, pushed, or put in fear, it is effectively a robbery. Snatch-thefts happen very quickly and often without any verbal interaction.
In many mugging incidents, the initial moments are critical: the mugger seeks to assert control over the victim to prevent resistance. This control can be achieved through a display of a weapon, a menacing threat, or a physical assault. If intimidation (e.g. simply brandishing a weapon or commanding compliance) succeeds, the mugger may obtain the valuables without further violence. If the victim resists or the “tough” posture fails, the assailant might resort to physical force to complete the robbery. Some muggings result in victims being knocked down, punched, kicked, or otherwise injured during the struggle.
Group tactics: While many muggers act alone, it is not uncommon for two or more offenders to work together. In a group mugging, one accomplice might restrain or distract the victim while another steals the valuables. A historical example of this is the garrote technique used by 19th-century street thieves: one attacker would choke the victim from behind, literally holding the person in a headlock, while an accomplice emptied the victim’s pockets or cut away a watch chain. Modern variations of group mugging might involve multiple youths surrounding a victim (sometimes called “steaming” in UK slang when gangs rob people in public places), or a pair on a motorbike where the passenger jumps off to snatch items. Working in teams can make the crime easier (one can handle the victim while the other grabs goods) and help offenders escape faster, but it also increases the chances of detection and later identification.
## Offenders and Victims
Offender profile: Street robberies are often perpetrated by young individuals. Studies in the United States have found that a large proportion of those arrested for robbery are teenagers or young adults in their early twenties. For example, in one analysis nearly half of robbery arrestees were under 21, and about two-thirds were under 25 years old. The crime is also overwhelmingly committed by males – police and victimization data worldwide consistently show that men constitute the majority of mugging perpetrators. Criminologists suggest various reasons for this demographic skew, including greater propensity of young men to engage in violent street crime due to social, economic, and opportunity factors.
Motive for muggings can range from immediate financial need to other factors. Often, the primary motive is quick money: offenders might be seeking cash to buy drugs or alcohol, to gain status items (clothes, electronics), or to pay debts. Some interviews with convicted street robbers indicate that the “quick cash” appeal is a major driver – robbery provides an immediate payoff without the need for elaborate planning. In some cases, especially with repeat offenders, there may also be a thrill or sense of power involved in overpowering a victim, but profit remains the key objective in most muggings (as opposed to assaults purely intended to harm someone).
Victim selection: Muggers typically select victims they perceive as vulnerable or unsuspecting. Characteristics that might attract a robber include apparent weakness (such as an elderly person or someone physically smaller), distraction (for instance, a person engrossed in looking at their phone or wearing headphones), isolation (walking alone at night or in a low-traffic area), and signs of wealth or good loot (carrying an expensive smartphone, jewelry, or cash). Tourists, intoxicated individuals, or people who seem unfamiliar with their surroundings are often targeted because they may be less alert or less likely to fight back. Criminals often watch for what police call “situational weakness” – any behavior or circumstance that makes an attack easier. For example, a robber might lurk near an ATM at night and target someone who has just withdrawn cash, or single out a pedestrian who is visibly nervous or lost. Conversely, individuals who walk confidently, stay alert to their environment, or are in groups can be less attractive targets to an opportunistic mugger.
Time and location: Street robberies are more likely to occur at certain times and places. Statistically, muggings happen most frequently under cover of darkness. Evenings and late nights (especially on weekends) are high-risk times for street crime, as there are more potential victims on the streets (patrons leaving bars, restaurants, nightclubs, etc.) and fewer people overall which can leave victims isolated. Criminological studies have noted clustering of street robberies around entertainment districts during weekend nights, after businesses have closed and foot traffic consists of people returning home who may be impaired or distracted. Residential neighborhoods can see muggings after dusk in areas that are poorly lit or deserted. Conversely, daylight incidents are less common but do occur in busy urban centers or wherever a perpetrator sees an opportunity (for example, a busy marketplace where a thief can use the crowd as cover to intimidate and then disappear).
In terms of location, urban areas have the highest incidence of mugging. The concentration of people, including both potential victims and potential offenders, in cities creates more opportunities. Within cities, certain hotspots such as dimly lit streets, parks, subway or bus stations, parking garages, and approaches to housing estates can have higher robbery rates. For instance, the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation reports that about one-third of all robberies nationally occur on public streets or highways (as opposed to indoors, in homes or businesses). In 2019, 34.3% of reported robberies in the United States took place on streets or sidewalks, making street muggings a major subset of robbery offenses. (By comparison, 15–20% of robberies happen in homes or private residences, and smaller percentages occur at commercial locations like stores, banks, or gas stations.) In some urban centers, the proportion of robberies that are street muggings is even higher. However, the exact patterns can vary by city and over time as law enforcement targets hotspots or as criminals shift tactics.
## Crime Rates and Trends
Prevalence: Mugging is a common form of violent crime in many parts of the world, contributing significantly to urban crime rates. It is difficult to quantify “muggings” globally, since official records classify them under robbery. However, data on robbery gives a picture of the trend. In the United States, the number of robberies (including street robberies) rose sharply in the late 1970s and 1980s, peaked in the early 1990s, and has since undergone a long-term decline. For example, in 1994 the U.S. robbery rate was about 6.3 per 1,000 inhabitants, but by 2005 this had fallen to 2.6 per 1,000. The downward trend continued into the 2010s. According to FBI statistics, there were an estimated 267,000 robberies nationwide in 2019, and by 2023 the annual number of reported robberies had further decreased to around 222,000 cases. This marks a dramatic reduction from the early 1990s, when over 600,000 robberies per year were recorded in the U.S. The decline in mugging and robbery rates has been attributed to multiple factors, including improved policing strategies, socioeconomic changes, and crime prevention measures (such as increased surveillance cameras and urban renewal reducing blighted areas).
It’s important to note that trends can differ by region. While the U.S. saw a drop in street robbery rates after the 1990s, other countries experienced different patterns. In England and Wales, for instance, police data showed robbery rates increasing in the late 1990s and early 2000s. A notable spike occurred around 2000–2002, partly attributed to a rise in mobile phone thefts and youth street crime. The media at that time frequently reported on “mobile phone muggings.” In response, British authorities implemented programs to curb street robbery in major cities, which eventually helped bring the rates down later in the 2000s.
Even within countries, urban centers tend to have higher mugging rates than rural areas. Large cities often account for a disproportionate share of robberies; for example, cities like New York, Los Angeles, London, and Paris each have neighborhoods where street muggings are more common, usually correlating with factors like higher population density, economic inequality, gang activity, or lower police presence. However, targeted law enforcement efforts can significantly impact local mugging rates. In New York City, street robbery occurrences fell dramatically from the 1990s to the 2010s alongside the city’s broader crime decline. Other cities have seen fluctuations—some experiencing increases in robbery during economic downturns or in the aftermath of reduced police patrols.
## Impact on Victims
Mugging is often described as a traumatic crime for the victim, not only because of the loss of property but especially due to the personal violation and threat to life involved. Unlike a non-violent theft (such as a pickpocketing), a mugging confronts victims with the fear of physical harm. Injuries are common in muggings, though the severity can vary widely. Studies indicate that about half of robbery victims are physically attacked in the incident (pushed, struck, or otherwise hurt), and roughly 20% of all robbery victims nationally require some form of medical treatment for injuries sustained. These injuries might include cuts, bruises, broken bones (from being knocked to the ground, for example), or more serious wounds if weapons were used. In a minority of cases, muggings can result in severe injuries or death, especially if the attacker is armed or if the victim resists forcefully. According to FBI data, around 5–6% of all homicides in the United States are robbery-related – meaning a robbery (which includes muggings) turned fatal for the victim. Firearms greatly increase the lethality of a mugging: while guns are used in less than one-third of robberies overall, they account for the majority of robbery-related deaths. Statistically, a robbery committed with a handgun or other firearm is several times more likely to result in the victim’s death compared to a robbery with a knife or blunt weapon. Because of this, many crime prevention experts advise victims who are confronted with an armed mugger not to resist and to comply with demands, since money and property can be replaced but life cannot.
Beyond physical harm, mugging can leave lasting psychological effects on victims. Being suddenly attacked and robbed often leads to trauma symptoms even if the physical injuries are minor. Victims frequently report heightened anxiety, fear, and loss of trust after such an incident. A study in the UK found that four out of five people who had been mugged or assaulted developed increased paranoia and mistrust of others in the months following the attack. Many victims experienced persistent fear of being out alone; for instance, some became afraid of strangers or felt unsafe in situations that previously did not trouble them. This kind of post-crime anxiety can be a form of post-traumatic stress. It’s not uncommon for mugging victims to have nightmares, flashbacks of the event, or to feel panicky when passing the location where the crime occurred. Some may avoid going out after dark or change their daily routines out of fear. Counseling and support groups for crime victims can help in recovering confidence and addressing the emotional fallout.
There is also a broader impact on the community’s sense of safety. A series of muggings in a neighborhood can create an atmosphere of fear among residents. People might alter their behavior – for example, avoiding certain streets, forming neighborhood watch groups, or demanding increased police patrols. Because muggings are visible and personal crimes, often reported in local news, they tend to influence public perceptions of crime more strongly than property crimes like burglary. Police often prioritize anti-mugging initiatives in response to public concern, as these crimes can erode quality of life and trust in public space if not addressed.
## Policing and Prevention
Law enforcement response: Police agencies combat mugging through a mix of traditional and specialized strategies. High-visibility patrols in robbery-prone areas (hotspots) are a common tactic – for example, deploying more officers on foot or in squad cars in neighborhoods or parks where muggings have occurred frequently. Some cities use targeted operations (decoy or “sting” operations) where undercover officers pose as potential victims to catch robbers in the act. Surveillance technology has also played a role: the installation of CCTV cameras in many city centers and transit stations provides deterrence and aids in identifying suspects after the fact. Improved street lighting and environmental design (such as cutting back overgrown shrubs or installing emergency call boxes) are preventive measures often employed by municipal authorities to make public spaces less conducive to ambush crimes. Studies have found that brighter street lighting in residential areas can reduce nighttime crimes, including robberies, by increasing visibility and natural surveillance. Community policing efforts, where officers engage with local residents and businesses, can encourage people to report suspicious behavior and help police identify patterns of repeat offenders who might be responsible for multiple muggings.
Because many muggings are committed by repeat offenders, law enforcement also focuses on apprehension and sentencing as deterrents. Once a mugger is caught, prosecutors typically pursue felony charges. Convictions for robbery can result in significant prison sentences – often several years to over a decade, and even more if a weapon was used or the victim was seriously injured. For example, a first-time offender convicted of unarmed robbery might receive a sentence on the order of 3–5 years in prison, whereas an armed robbery conviction can bring 10–20 years or more, depending on jurisdiction. Some regions have “three strikes” laws or specific mandatory minimum sentences that apply to violent repeat offenders, which can lead to life sentences for serial muggers. The rationale is that strong penalties will discourage potential offenders (a principle of deterrence) and incapacitate those who are most dangerous. However, the effectiveness of harsh sentencing on preventing street-level robberies is debated in criminal justice circles, with some experts arguing that addressing root causes (like drug addiction or economic desperation) is also necessary to reduce mugging rates.
Personal prevention: Public education on how to reduce one’s risk of being mugged is another aspect of prevention. Police and safety organizations often suggest common-sense precautions, such as traveling in groups at night, staying in well-lit areas, keeping valuables out of sight (for instance, not openly displaying an expensive phone or large amounts of cash), and remaining aware of one’s surroundings. Individuals are advised to trust their instincts – if they feel uneasy about a person or location, it may be best to avoid it. Self-defense classes and tools (like personal alarms or pepper spray, where legal) are sometimes promoted, but authorities typically emphasize that no resistance is the safest approach if one is actually confronted by a mugger with a weapon. Handing over one’s wallet or phone is preferable to risking violent escalation. After a mugging incident, police urge victims to report the crime as soon as possible, provide descriptions of the attacker, and cancel stolen credit cards or phones quickly to mitigate further harm.
Overall, while mugging remains a serious street crime around the world, its incidence has declined in many places since its peak in the late 20th century. Ongoing efforts by law enforcement, urban planners, and communities aim to continue that trend by making public spaces safer and reducing the opportunities and incentives for would-be muggers.

While the U.S. saw a drop in street robbery rates after the 1990s, other countries experienced different patterns.
In England and Wales, police data showed robbery rates increasing in the late 1990s and early 2000s.
A notable spike in robbery rates occurred around 2000–2002 in England and Wales.
The spike in robbery rates around 2000-2002 in England and Wales was partly attributed to a rise in mobile phone thefts and youth street crime.
The media at that time frequently reported on “mobile phone muggings”.
In response to rising robbery rates, British authorities implemented programs to curb street robbery in major cities.
These programs eventually helped bring the rates down later in the 2000s.
Even within countries, urban centers tend to have higher mugging rates than rural areas.
Large cities often account for a disproportionate share of robberies.
Cities like New York, Los Angeles, London, and Paris each have neighborhoods where street muggings are more common.
Higher mugging rates usually correlate with factors like higher population density, economic inequality, gang activity, or lower police presence.
Targeted law enforcement efforts can significantly impact local mugging rates.
In New York City, street robbery occurrences fell dramatically from the 1990s to the 2010s alongside the city’s broader crime decline.
Other cities have seen fluctuations in robbery rates.
Some cities experience increases in robbery during economic downturns or in the aftermath of reduced police patrols.
Mugging is often described as a traumatic crime for the victim.
Mugging is traumatic not only because of the loss of property but especially due to the personal violation and threat to life involved.
Unlike a non-violent theft (such as a pickpocketing), a mugging confronts victims with the fear of physical harm.
Injuries are common in muggings, though the severity can vary widely.
Studies indicate that about half of robbery victims are physically attacked in the incident (pushed, struck, or otherwise hurt).
Roughly 20% of all robbery victims nationally require some form of medical treatment for injuries sustained.
Injuries from muggings might include cuts, bruises, broken bones (from being knocked to the ground, for example), or more serious wounds if weapons were used.
In a minority of cases, muggings can result in severe injuries or death, especially if the attacker is armed or if the victim resists forcefully.
According to FBI data, around 5–6% of all homicides in the United States are robbery-related.
Robbery-related homicides mean a robbery (which includes muggings) turned fatal for the victim.
Firearms greatly increase the lethality of a mugging.
While guns are used in less than one-third of robberies overall, they account for the majority of robbery-related deaths.
Statistically, a robbery committed with a handgun or other firearm is several times more likely to result in the victim’s death compared to a robbery with a knife or blunt weapon.
Many crime prevention experts advise victims who are confronted with an armed mugger not to resist and to comply with demands.
Money and property can be replaced but life cannot.
Beyond physical harm, mugging can leave lasting psychological effects on victims.
Being suddenly attacked and robbed often leads to trauma symptoms even if the physical injuries are minor.
Victims frequently report heightened anxiety, fear, and loss of trust after such an incident.
A study in the UK found that four out of five people who had been mugged or assaulted developed increased paranoia and mistrust of others in the months following the attack.
Many victims experienced persistent fear of being out alone.
Some mugging victims became afraid of strangers or felt unsafe in situations that previously did not trouble them.
Post-crime anxiety can be a form of post-traumatic stress.
It’s not uncommon for mugging victims to have nightmares, flashbacks of the event, or to feel panicky when passing the location where the crime occurred.
Some mugging victims may avoid going out after dark or change their daily routines out of fear.
Counseling and support groups for crime victims can help in recovering confidence and addressing the emotional fallout.
There is also a broader impact on the community’s sense of safety from muggings.
A series of muggings in a neighborhood can create an atmosphere of fear among residents.
People might alter their behavior, for example, avoiding certain streets, forming neighborhood watch groups, or demanding increased police patrols.
Because muggings are visible and personal crimes, often reported in local news, they tend to influence public perceptions of crime more strongly than property crimes like burglary.
Police often prioritize anti-mugging initiatives in response to public concern.
Muggings can erode quality of life and trust in public space if not addressed.
Police agencies combat mugging through a mix of traditional and specialized strategies.
High-visibility patrols in robbery-prone areas (hotspots) are a common tactic.
Deploying more officers on foot or in squad cars in neighborhoods or parks where muggings have occurred frequently is an example of high-visibility patrols.
Some cities use targeted operations (decoy or “sting” operations) where undercover officers pose as potential victims to catch robbers in the act.
Surveillance technology has played a role in combating mugging.
The installation of CCTV cameras in many city centers and transit stations provides deterrence and aids in identifying suspects after the fact.

Improved street lighting and environmental design (such as cutting back overgrown shrubs or installing emergency call boxes) are preventive measures often employed by municipal authorities to make public spaces less conducive to ambush crimes.
Studies have found that brighter street lighting in residential areas can reduce nighttime crimes, including robberies, by increasing visibility and natural surveillance.
Community policing efforts, where officers engage with local residents and businesses, can encourage people to report suspicious behavior.
Community policing efforts can help police identify patterns of repeat offenders who might be responsible for multiple muggings.
Many muggings are committed by repeat offenders.
Law enforcement focuses on apprehension and sentencing as deterrents for muggings.
Once a mugger is caught, prosecutors typically pursue felony charges.
Convictions for robbery can result in significant prison sentences.
Prison sentences for robbery are often several years to over a decade.
Prison sentences for robbery can be even more if a weapon was used or the victim was seriously injured.
A first-time offender convicted of unarmed robbery might receive a sentence on the order of 3–5 years in prison.
An armed robbery conviction can bring 10–20 years or more, depending on jurisdiction.
Some regions have “three strikes” laws or specific mandatory minimum sentences that apply to violent repeat offenders.
“Three strikes” laws or specific mandatory minimum sentences can lead to life sentences for serial muggers.
The rationale for strong penalties is that they will discourage potential offenders (a principle of deterrence) and incapacitate those who are most dangerous.
The effectiveness of harsh sentencing on preventing street-level robberies is debated in criminal justice circles.
Some experts argue that addressing root causes (like drug addiction or economic desperation) is also necessary to reduce mugging rates.
Public education on how to reduce one’s risk of being mugged is another aspect of prevention.

Police and safety organizations often suggest common-sense precautions, such as traveling in groups at night, staying in well-lit areas, keeping valuables out of sight (for instance, not openly displaying an expensive phone or large amounts of cash), and remaining aware of one’s surroundings.
Individuals are advised to trust their instincts.
If individuals feel uneasy about a person or location, it may be best to avoid it.
Self-defense classes and tools (like personal alarms or pepper spray, where legal) are sometimes promoted.
Authorities typically emphasize that no resistance is the safest approach if one is actually confronted by a mugger with a weapon.
Handing over one’s wallet or phone is preferable to risking violent escalation.
After a mugging incident, police urge victims to report the crime as soon as possible.
After a mugging incident, police urge victims to provide descriptions of the attacker.
After a mugging incident, police urge victims to cancel stolen credit cards or phones quickly to mitigate further harm.
Mugging remains a serious street crime around the world.
The incidence of mugging has declined in many places since its peak in the late 20th century.
Ongoing efforts by law enforcement, urban planners, and communities aim to continue the trend of declining mugging incidence.
Ongoing efforts aim to make public spaces safer and reduce the opportunities and incentives for would-be muggers.

3.6 Activity: Mugging and the media
===================================

In 1978 Stuart Hall and his co-writers (Chas Critcher, Tony Jefferson, John Clarke and Brian Roberts) published _Policing the Crisis: Mugging, the State and Law and Order_, in which they argued that the growth in media coverage of crime in Britain in the early 1970s contributed to a widespread belief that there was a crisis in society, in particular to do with the sudden rise of the ‘mugger’ or street robber. The video with Professor Stuart Hall which you are now going to watch is introduced by one of Hall’s co-authors, Professor John Clarke.

#### Transcript: The media and social disorder

JOHN CLARK

Hello, I’m John Clark. And I’m here to explore the relationship between the media and a social problem, like juvenile delinquency, to see how some types of behaviour, and some types of people, come to be labelled as ‘disorderly’. The video you’re about to watch looks at the relationship between the media, the public, and what it calls ‘primary definers’ – people like the police, judges and politicians – to see how they act together to define some sorts of people and behaviour as disorderly.

The video, presented by Stuart Hall, was made in 1975 and explores some of the work that he and his colleagues did for a book called Policing the Crisis. As you watch the video, you might want to think about why a video, made in the 1970s, makes sense for social sciences now.

STUART HALL

Twenty years is a long time for a boy of sixteen. And the fact that he’s weeping in court doesn’t suggest that he’s a hardened criminal. Well, between August 1972 and October ’73, Britain experienced a wave of muggings – ‘robberies following sudden attacks in the open,’ as they’ve been officially defined. And this mugging epidemic got widespread coverage in the press.

In this programme, we want to look at the relation between the mass media and a social problem like mugging. Now, the common sense view is that the mugging outbreak was sudden and unexpected. Muggings happened. The press reported them.

When the wave of muggings receded, the coverage decreased. So the main constraints seemed to be technical ones – getting the facts, presenting them fast and accurately, reporting the experts, expressing editorial views, and so on. In fact, we’ll try to show that the relation of the media to social problems isn’t so simple. And the main constraints aren’t technical, but social.

But first, the label itself – ‘mugging’. In law, there’s actually no such crime. And there’s no figure for it in the statistics until 1973. No actual British crime is called a mugging until August 1972.

Let’s take an example. Here are two news stories, both about someone attacked in the open – one before August 1972, one after. One difference between them is clearly the size of the coverage. That’s a front page and that’s a lead story.

Another difference is the use, but in the second story only, of the ‘mugging’ label. It’s the size of the sentence and the mugging label that has attracted the attention. And the picture of the judge lends the item weight.

Now the media tend to work with labels like that. And labels simplify. They identify. They mark things out and they focus our attention on things. ‘Teddy boy’ – ‘hell’s angel’ – ‘skinhead’.

One man’s urban terrorist is another man’s freedom fighter. Labels mobilise strong feelings and attitudes. They carry a lot of moral weight. They help us to make sense of things. And they give people personal qualities.

But they also help to cluster stories in the press which don’t necessarily belong together. And the more stories there are about the same kind of crime or disaster, the bigger the coverage. So labels help to create a sort of news spiral. But where, in fact, did this label – ‘mugging’ – come from?

\[POLICE SIREN\]

\[POLICE SIREN\]

\[POLICE SIREN\]

Well, must Harlem come to Handsworth? It’s quite common in the British media to find stories about America used as a sort of early warning device. In each of his three big speeches about immigration, for example, Enoch Powell used America as the basis of a prediction and warning about Britain. And pictures and stories like the ones we’ve just seen taught us the meaning of a word like ‘mugging’.

They sensitise us to mugging even before muggings appear. They give us an image of what sort of mugger to expect – his race, his city background. We could build up a sort of identity-kit picture of him from these stories. His home is in the poor parts of the city. He’s probably black.

He’d be vicious. There’d probably be a connection with drugs. His victims would be elderly and vulnerable. He has a taste for violence, for kicks. He’s part of a larger pattern of lawlessness – the breakdown of law and order.

In this interview, Sir Robert Mark draws the attention of the interviewer to the mugging statistics which are in his report. He defines it. He also interprets the meaning of the bare figures and he points up the focusing of police activity in certain areas.

SIR ROBERT MARK

Yes, I think – it’s subdivided, I think, as between robberies in the streets against inoffensive people.

INTERVIEWER

Mugging, you mean?

SIR ROBERT MARK

Mugging – well, they’re vulgarly known as muggings, but they’re really robberies. Or occasionally, I suppose, they come under the heading of thefts from the person. That’s one category. The second category, of course, is the deliberate, planned, sophisticated crime against banks and payrolls. These are two very serious problems, of course.

INTERVIEWER

There were a lot last year, bank raids. How about this year?

SIR ROBERT MARK

Well, we’ve had a period of regrouping and reorganisation. And during that period, we have made a great effort to identify our targets and to direct our resources against them. And the result of this is that I think, although one must never be too optimistic, but in relation to robberies in the streets, there is an encouraging fall. And in relation to bank raids, I think it’s even more encouraging that the number of these has fallen from seven a month in the first six months of last year to rather less than three a month in the equivalent period of this year.

STUART HALL

The media love the crime statistics because they tend to go for hard facts. And there’s no fact so hard as a number, unless it’s the percentage difference between two numbers. But the crime statistics are, indeed, notoriously hard to interpret. Here’s the graph for the general category of robbery, from the annual crime figures for the metropolitan area.

Now here’s the figure for mugging. There’s no published figure for mugging before 1972. Later, the mugging figures are projected back to 1968. Strictly speaking, the 1968 figure is for a crime which, at the time, probably wasn’t called mugging at all, and it may include mugging-type crimes which are derived from other robbery categories.

So the mugging label has played a part here too in clustering crimes under the mugging heading. Here’s a related figure for a kind of robbery which sounds rather like mugging. But there’s no figure given for ‘snatchings in the open’ after 1969.

If you look at another crime, rather like mugging, theft from the person – or snatching – well, it’s even higher in 1972 than the mugging figure. Well, this isn’t a programme about crime statistics. But it is worth remembering that the hard facts behind headlines like ‘Muggings go up 129 per cent’ aren’t as simple, or as hard, as they seem.

One can see the image of mugging there on its way from the police spokesman to the television interviewer. The image is already familiar. The mugger is callous, violent, he attacks the weak and vulnerable. He robs for kicks rather than for gain.

Naturally, certain features which fall outside this image don’t get reported. Now the general public is sensitised to mugging via this image. And they then express fears about mugging, perhaps in letters to the press. And judges who are deciding on a sentence refer to this public anxiety.

The sentences get longer. This in itself is newsworthy. It becomes a news story. And it refocuses public attention.

This is an amplification spiral. And the media don’t stand outside this spiral, they form part of it. Each aspect of the public debate about mugging passes through the media. They form the link between the definers and controllers, the public, and the news.

JOHN CLARK

Stuart Hall explains how the media work with images and labels to simplify social issues and to cluster new stories together. This clustering of news about crime then creates public anxiety. In turn, politicians, police, judges, respond to this public anxiety and escalate the issue. This causes what Hall calls an ‘amplification spiral’.

The key point here is the role of the media within this spiral. The media do not stand outside the spiral. Rather, they are the critical link between the public, the news stories and the primary definers. But why might any of this be relevant today, at a time when news stories about mugging are thin on the ground?

I was recently involved in producing an updated version of Policing the Crisis. And I think that its central message remains as relevant today as it was when the book was first written. The media still play a crucial role in labelling certain sorts of behaviour and certain types of people in ways that generate public anxiety. Today’s moral panics might not be about muggers. They might be about benefit scroungers or rioters. But the media continue to play this central role in generating moral panics.

Robbery
=======

[Download Printable Document](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/topic-pages/robbery.pdf)

### **Definition**

The FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting (UCR) Program defines robbery as the taking or attempting to take anything of value from the care, custody, or control of a person or persons by force or threat of force or violence and/or by putting the victim in fear.

### **Overview  
**

*   There were an estimated 267,988 robberies nationwide in 2019. The estimated number of robberies decreased 4.7 percent from the 2018 estimate and decreased 18.3 percent from the 2015 estimate. The 2019 estimate was down 27.4 percent from the 2010 estimate. (See Tables **[1](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-1)** and **[1A](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-1/table-1a)**.)

*   The estimated robbery rate of 81.6 per 100,000 inhabitants in 2019 showed a decrease of 5.2 percent when compared with the 2018 rate. (See Tables **[1](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-1)** and **[1A](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-1/table-1a)**.)

*   In 2019, the average dollar value of property stolen per reported robbery was $1,797. Robberies accounted for an estimated $482 million in losses. Banks experienced the highest average dollar loss at $4,213 per offense. (Based on Tables **[1](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-1)** and **[23](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-23)**.)

*   Among the robberies for which the UCR Program received weapon information in 2019, strong-arm tactics were used in 44.8 percent, firearms in 36.4 percent, and knives or cutting instruments in 8.5 percent. Other dangerous weapons were used in 10.3 percent of robberies in 2019. (Based on **[Table 19](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-19)**.)

### **Expanded data  
**

Expanded offense data are the details of the various offenses that the UCR Program collects beyond the count of how many crimes law enforcement agencies report. These details may include the type of weapon used in a crime, type or value of items stolen, and so forth. In addition, expanded data include trends (for example, 2-year comparisons) and rates per 100,000 inhabitants.

Expanded information regarding robbery is available in the following tables:

*   Trends (2-year): Tables **[12](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-12)**, **[13](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-13)**, **[14](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-14)**, and **[15](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-15)**

*   Rates (per 100,000 inhabitants): Tables **[16](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-16)**, **[17](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-17)**, **[18](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-18)**, and **[19](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-19)**

*   Weapons: Tables **[15](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-15)**, **[19](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-19)**, and **[21](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-21)**

*   Location Type, average value of items stolen by location per robbery: **[Table 23](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/table-23)**

*   [**Robbery Table 1**](https://ucr.fbi.gov/crime-in-the-u.s/2019/crime-in-the-u.s.-2019/tables/robbery-table-1.xls), “Robbery, Location, Percent Distribution by Region, 2019”

### **Robbery Location Figure**

This figure is a pie chart that shows the percentages of robbery offenses by location type in 2019. In the nation, 34.3 percent of robbery offenses occurred on streets or highways, 16.7 percent occurred at commercial houses, 15.8 percent occurred at residences, 6.6 percent occurred at convenience stores, 3.0 percent occurred at gas or service stations, 1.4 percent occurred at banks, and 22.2 percent occurred at miscellaneous locations.
